claims.reason: Only the general direction is backed: the NHS page tells the reader to see a GP when changing sleeping habits has not helped and the problem affects daily life (lines 145 and 149, listed as symptoms of insomnia, including still feeling tired after waking up on line 25). Not backed: the trigger stated in the sentence (significant sleepiness despite adequate opportunity to sleep) is not the NHS condition (trouble sleeping), and neither snapshot says to consult 'instead of' increasing caffeine; the NHS page mentions caffeine only as a cause of insomnia (line 61) and coffee or tea only as something to avoid in the 6 hours before bed (line 117). The Van Dongen abstract is silent on consulting anyone. NHS line 47 says constant daytime tiredness probably means too little sleep, which does not address the sentence's case either.

claims.reason: The grade letter B is editorial and was not checked. The words after it describe the sources. Laboratory setting and the NHS general information on sleep need (lines 35-47) are confirmed. Randomization is named in the abstract only for the chronic sleep restriction experiment (4/6/8 h); the abstract says nothing about randomization in the total sleep deprivation experiment, while the sentence says 'badania ... z randomizacją' in the plural. The evidence is an abstract only (Europe PMC), so the full text would be needed to settle this.

quotes.text: wake up several times during the night
still feel tired after waking up

claims.reason: Neither snapshot states in general that sleep quality matters in addition to duration. The NHS page only lists fragmented sleep and waking up still tired among the symptoms of insomnia (lines 19 and 25), which implies that quality counts but does not say so. The Van Dongen abstract concerns time in bed and polysomnographic markers, not sleep quality as a determinant of need.

claims.claim: Badanie nie określa dokładnej potrzeby każdej osoby
claims.reason: This is a claim of absence about the Van Dongen study. The snapshot is only the abstract, which describes fixed doses (4, 6, 8 h) assigned by randomization and group-level results, and does not say whether individual sleep need was estimated. Absence cannot be shown from an abstract. The full text would be needed.

claims.claim: nie uzasadnia samodzielnego leczenia zaburzeń snu

scope_gaps.note: The title generalises from forced laboratory sleep restriction in healthy adults aged 21-38 to everyday planning. The abstract reports that subjective sleepiness ratings rose acutely and then only slightly while performance kept falling; it does not test whether a person who feels not sleepy is rested. The NHS page (line 47) goes the other way: constant daytime tiredness probably means too little sleep.
'przez 14 dni' attaches to the 4/6/8 h restriction arms. The total sleep deprivation experiment lasted 3 nights (abstract), which the sentence does not state; a reader might assume 14 days for both.

Deficits and the gap between ratings and performance were measured under imposed laboratory restriction in healthy adults, not in people who habitually sleep little at home. The sentence does not claim otherwise.
The NHS 'See a GP' advice concerns insomnia (trouble sleeping), not significant daytime sleepiness despite adequate time for sleep, and has nothing on caffeine as a substitute for consulting.
Randomization is stated in the abstract only for the chronic restriction experiment, not for the total sleep deprivation experiment; the sentence uses the plural 'badania'.
The abstract-only snapshot cannot show what the study did not determine; the second part (self-treatment) is not a claim from either source and is derived from the population and design rows.
